youtube.baslik: How Sound Travels from the Ear to the Brain | Lesson 03 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
We follow a sound step by step, from the auricle to the auditory cortex. We explain the roles of the outer, middle and inner ear, how vibration becomes a neural signal, and what the brainstem and the cortex do.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; Gelfand, Hearing: An Introduction to Psychological and Physiological Acoustics; Pickles, An Introduction to the Physiology of Hearing; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.baslik: How Sound Travels from the Ear to the *Brain*
sahneler.alt: Outer, middle and inner ear, brainstem and cortex
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson, we follow the path of a sound from start to finish, from the auricle to the brain.
We will see the roles of the outer, middle and inner ear, how vibration becomes a neural signal, and how the brain processes it.
Anatomically, the ear is divided into three parts.
The first is the auris externa, or outer ear, made up of the auricle and the external auditory canal.
The second is the auris media, or middle ear, the air-filled space behind the tympanic membrane.
The third is the auris interna, or inner ear, a fluid-filled structure deep inside the temporal bone.
The inner ear contains both the cochlea, the organ of hearing, and the vestibular system, the organ of balance.
On this journey, sound is first a vibration in air, then a mechanical vibration, then a fluid wave and finally a neural signal.
The sound wave first reaches the auricle, which collects the sound and directs it into the ear canal.
The external auditory canal is a slightly S-shaped channel about two point five centimeters long.
This canal acts like a tube closed at one end and boosts sounds between about two thousand and four thousand hertz.
Together, the auricle and the canal provide a gain of about ten to twenty decibels in this region.
The folds of the auricle create cues that help us tell whether a sound comes from the front or from behind.
Earwax and the structure of the canal protect the ear from foreign bodies and infection.
Many consonants that are important for understanding speech also lie in this boosted frequency region.
At the end of the ear canal lies the tympanic membrane, or eardrum.
When the sound wave strikes it, the tympanic membrane vibrates in step with the frequency of the sound.
This vibration is carried by the ossicles, the tiny bones of the ear: first the malleus, then the incus.
The last link in the chain is the stapes, the smallest bone in the human body.
The footplate of the stapes sits in the oval window, the entrance to the inner ear, and passes the vibration into the inner ear fluid.
The middle ear is filled with air and connects to the back of the nose, the nasopharynx, through the Eustachian tube.
The Eustachian tube equalizes the air pressure in the middle ear with the outside environment.

sahneler.baslik: Why do we *need* a middle ear?
cumleler: The inner ear is filled with fluid, and when sound passes from air into fluid, most of its energy is reflected back.
Without the middle ear, this reflection would cause a loss of about thirty decibels.
The middle ear solves this in two ways; first, the tympanic membrane is about seventeen times larger than the stapes footplate.
Second, the ossicular chain works like a small lever and increases the force by about one point three times.
Together, these mechanisms provide a gain of about twenty five to thirty decibels; this is called impedance matching.
We will cover this topic in detail in the physiology lessons.
As the stapes pushes the oval window in and pulls it back, pressure waves form in the fluid of the cochlea.
Because fluid cannot be compressed, this movement is balanced by the round window at the base bulging the opposite way.
The basilar membrane, which runs along the cochlea, starts to vibrate with this fluid movement.
The vibration forms a traveling wave that moves from the base toward the apex.
High-pitched sounds produce their largest vibration near the base of the cochlea.
Low-pitched sounds travel all the way toward the apex; this frequency map is called tonotopy.
In this way, the cochlea splits incoming sound into its components, like a frequency analyzer.
The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane, and this is where the actual conversion takes place.
The inner hair cells in the organ of Corti are the true sensory cells that pass auditory information to the nerve.
When the membrane vibrates, the fine projections on top of the hair cells, the stereocilia, bend.
This bending opens ion channels in the cell, and mechanical energy is turned into an electrical signal.
The outer hair cells lengthen and shorten, which amplifies soft sounds and sharpens frequency selectivity.
The nerve fibers stimulated by the inner hair cells carry this signal to the auditory nerve.

ogeler.metin: Firing rate and number of fibers

cumleler: The auditory nerve carries frequency mainly by a place code; each fiber brings information from a specific region of the cochlea.
In this way, each of the roughly thirty thousand fibers is tuned to its own frequency.
For low-pitched sounds, fibers also fire at particular phases of the sound wave; this is called phase locking.
As a sound gets louder, the firing rate of the fibers rises and more fibers are recruited.
From these codes, the brain decodes both the pitch and the loudness of a sound.
Sound can reach the cochlea not only through the air but also through vibration of the skull bones.
This is called bone conduction; on this route, the outer and middle ear are largely bypassed.
One reason our recorded voice sounds different is that, when we speak, we also hear ourselves by bone conduction.
In the clinic, bone conduction testing lets us see the state of the cochlea and beyond, separately from air conduction.
This difference is the basis for telling apart the types of hearing loss, the topic of the next lesson.
The signal reaches the brainstem through the auditory nerve, the eighth cranial nerve.
The first stop is the cochlear nucleus; the fibers arriving here come only from the ear on the same side.
Next comes the superior olivary complex, where information from the two ears is compared for the first time.
The signal rises along the lateral lemniscus and reaches the inferior colliculus in the midbrain.
The medial geniculate body in the thalamus is the last relay station that passes the signal on to the cortex.
Finally, the signal reaches the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.
Along the way, most fibers cross to the opposite side, so each ear is represented in both halves of the brain.
The brainstem does not only relay the signal; it also processes it.
In the superior olivary complex, the time and intensity differences of sound reaching the two ears are compared.
This is how we can work out which direction a sound comes from.
The acoustic reflex, which contracts the stapedius muscle in the middle ear for loud sounds, also works at the brainstem level.
Fibers running down from the brain to the ear act on the outer hair cells and help with listening in noise.
The auditory brainstem response, or ABR, which we will see later, measures electrical activity in the early parts of this pathway.
The last stop on the pathway is the primary auditory cortex.
This area lies on the upper surface of the temporal lobe, in a region called Heschl's gyrus.
The frequency map that began in the cochlea is preserved here; different frequencies are represented in different areas of the cortex.
Recognizing whether a sound is a word or music happens together with the surrounding auditory association areas.
For understanding speech, Wernicke's area in the left hemisphere plays an important role in most people.
In short, the ear receives and codes the sound, but it is the brain that understands what we hear.
Now let us bring the whole journey together in one picture.
In the outer ear, sound is still an acoustic wave in the air; the auricle and canal collect and boost it.
In the middle ear, the energy becomes mechanical vibration and is matched for transfer into fluid.
In the inner ear, the fluid wave vibrates the basilar membrane, and the hair cells turn this into an electrical signal.
The neural pathways and the cortex then transmit, process and make sense of this signal.

sahneler.metin: Think about which part of the pathway each test measures: tympanometry shows the middle ear, OAE the outer hair cells, ABR the auditory nerve and brainstem.
cumleler: This road map is very useful in the clinic.
When you interpret a test result, think about which part of the pathway the test measures.
Tympanometry assesses the middle ear, and otoacoustic emissions, or OAE, assess the outer hair cells.
The ABR assesses the auditory nerve and the brainstem pathways.
Interpreting these tests together is the most reliable way to locate the problem.
The outer ear collects and directs sound and boosts the frequencies that matter for speech.
The middle ear transfers sound in air efficiently into the fluid-filled inner ear.
The cochlea splits sound into its frequencies, and the hair cells turn vibration into a neural signal.
The brainstem processes sound and finds its direction, and the cortex makes sense of what we hear.

sahneler.soru: Where is information from the two ears first compared?
sahneler.aciklama: The _superior olivary complex_ is the first stop where input from both ears comes together; it is key for localization.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: Where in the auditory pathway is information from the two ears first compared?

cumleler: The correct answer is B, the superior olivary complex. The cochlear nucleus receives input only from the ear on the same side.
Information from the two ears first meets in the superior olivary complex and is used to localize sound.
In the next lesson, we will learn the types of hearing loss, based on which part of this pathway is affected.
